headline: US Treasury buyback intervention failed to calm bond market as structural debt dynamics overwhelm liquidity tools
reasoning: Scott Bessent's US$4 billion Treasury buyback program, which doubled the maximum size of planned buybacks of 10-to-30-year bonds, produced only a temporary rally before yields resumed rising and USD-denominated assets weakened. Stanley Druckenmiller argued the market was functioning normally — investors were simply demanding higher yields to absorb America's growing debt — and that 'you can't buy your way out of a solvency conversation with liquidity tools.' The intervention risked blurring the line between liquidity support and yield curve control. US Treasury yields set the global price of money, with knock-on effects across equities, bonds, property and infrastructure worldwide, including Australian portfolios.
quote: With long-term yields surging, the Treasury unexpectedly doubled the maximum size of planned buybacks of 10-to-30-year bonds. Bessent's move was an expansion of the Treasury's existing liquidity-support program, not yield curve control, where a central bank targets a particular bond yield and buys whatever amount is needed to defend it. Nevertheless, veteran macro investor Stanley Druckenmiller argues that its timing risked blurring the line between supporting liquidity and influencing prices. Writing in The Wall Street Journal, he said the market was functioning; investors were simply demanding higher yields to absorb America's growing debt. As he put it, 'you can't buy your way out of a solvency conversation with liquidity tools.'
